$comment: VENDORED copy of the normative kiosk.tech schema at spec/schemas/schema-descriptor.schema.json. It is here so e2e/schema_conformance.rb can validate this origin's LIVE wire bytes against the PUBLISHED schema with no second checkout and no network fetch (K-822). Identical to the upstream copy as PARSED JSON once this $comment is removed — bin/check-spec-schemas asserts exactly that whenever the umbrella layout puts kiosk.tech next to this repo, and says so rather than pretending when it does not. T-045 tracks the sync-check.
title: Kiosk schema descriptor
description: The body returned by GET <endpoint>/schema. UNAUTHENTICATED: the catalog is public. It carries the origin's verbs and their contracts and nothing else -- the MODULE set it once duplicated as `verbs` lives in `capabilities` in /.well-known/kiosk.json, which is where an AI assistant reads it. The root is CLOSED: a document carrying `verbs`, or any other key this schema does not declare, is not a conformant catalog.

descriptor.description: One verb's description. CLOSED (K-1278, Section 8.3): a descriptor carries the members named here and no others, so a key this specification does not declare at this level -- `x_internal_sla`, `ttl`, an operator's internal owner -- makes the catalog non-conformant. An operator that wants a field on a verb proposes it for the protocol rather than publishing it: a name taken privately is a name a later revision can no longer claim. This closes the DESCRIPTOR and nothing else; a problem document still carries its RFC 9457 extension members, which is that object's own rule.

name.description: The verb's wire name, which is also its path segment under `endpoint`. One name is one KIND: a name listed under `queries` must not also appear under `actions`.

description.description: Human-facing description or null. SEMANTICS live here in prose -- what the verb does, when to reach for it, what the result means. Names, types and constraints do not: an input belongs to input_schema and a result field to output_schema.

reach.description: REQUIRED. Whose rows this verb may touch (Section 7.2). `principal` is the DEFAULT and the norm: this verb touches only the calling principal's own rows, or rows that belong to no principal at all (a catalogue, a price list). The other three are DECLARED DEPARTURES, each naming what authorises the wider reach -- `published`, the operator publishes these owner-carrying rows to every principal by intent (a classifieds board); `consented`, a principal shared them and the operator can point at the artefact that says so (an invite that became a membership) -- the stronger of the two sharing claims; `role`, the reach follows the caller's operator-ASSIGNED `role` claim, which is never client-requested (Section 5.4). Declaring a reach does not make it correct, it makes it reviewable: an UNDECLARED cross-principal read is a defect whether or not the operator intended it. An AI assistant that meets a descriptor with no `reach` MUST read the verb as `principal` and MUST NOT take the absence as licence to assume anything wider.

input_schema.description: REQUIRED. JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) for THIS verb's inputs: names, required/optional, types, enums, ranges. The AUTHORITATIVE input contract -- the only place a parameter name is declared -- and it wins over any `description` sentence that disagrees. The operator validates a request's arguments against it before the handler runs and answers 400 bad_request naming the offending parameter otherwise. A verb that takes nothing declares the closed empty object.

output_schema.description: REQUIRED. JSON Schema (draft 2020-12) for what this verb RETURNS. With no response envelope, this is the ONLY machine-readable statement of the result shape: what a query's rows look like, or what an action's object contains. A query's is an ARRAY schema whether or not the verb paginates -- a paginated page carries its cursor in an RFC 8288 Link header, not in the body -- so a paginating verb declares one shape, not a two-branch union. It must describe what the verb actually renders -- a success body that does not satisfy it is an operator-side defect, not a permitted variation.

params.description: FORBIDDEN. `false` refuses the key outright: the retired 0.3 free-form hint object was WITHDRAWN from the wire in 0.4 (Section 8.3), and a catalog that still publishes one -- including the `null` every 0.3 origin published -- is not conformant. It keeps its own declaration now that the object around it is closed, and the redundancy is only apparent: `additionalProperties` does not reach a key `properties` names, so a descriptor still publishing `params` is refused by THIS sentence, which says what was withdrawn and when, rather than by the generic unknown-member refusal every other stray key gets. Contrast the ROOT, closed for the same reason and saying so above.

example_params.description: OPTIONAL example params object an AI assistant can copy verbatim as a starting call for this verb. It ILLUSTRATES input_schema and is not the contract: where the two disagree, the schema is right.

example_row.description: OPTIONAL example of one result element -- a representative row for a query, or the example return value for an action. It ILLUSTRATES output_schema and is not the contract.
